beats.vo: Your onion shoots tiny droplets when you cut it.
beats.visual: Overhead on a warm countertop: a matte, chunky yellow onion half under a steel blade edge. The blade drops and a fan of bright droplets sprays up in slow motion, backlit by window light. Reads in under 2 s.

beats.vo: One lab caught it on cameras far faster than your eyes can see.
beats.visual: Cut to a side-on macro of the blade meeting the onion skin, shown in ultra slow motion with a tiny frame counter ticking at the edge. Overhead lens lowers to counter level (motivated: to see the splash).

beats.vo: Droplets burst out at up to about ninety miles an hour.
beats.visual: Follow a single droplet from the cut as it streaks up and away across the frame; a small speed number counts up beside it. Camera tracks the drop (follow).

beats.vo: That was a lab rig that drops a blade onto half an onion, not a chef.
beats.visual: Pull back to reveal a clean steel guillotine rig with a vertical slider holding the blade over a half onion on the countertop. Slow overhead pull-back.

beats.vo: Within a fiftieth of a second, they split into hundreds, even thousands, of smaller drops.
beats.visual: Macro of one big droplet bursting into a fine mist of smaller ones in slow motion, each catching a speck of light. Static macro, no shake.

beats.vo: Why cry? Cutting breaks open the cells. A reaction turns the onion's sulfur compounds into an eye irritant.
beats.visual: Camera drops straight down into the cut surface to cell scale: cells split, chunky yellow sulfur molecules react and form a small Tomato-red irritant shape. Motivated drop on the break.

beats.vo: It switches on nerves in your cornea, the clear front of your eye. Tears.
beats.visual: Overhead cutaway to a stylised eye: the irritant shape touches the clear dome and a nerve lights; a tear bead forms and rolls. Slow push-in on the cornea.

beats.vo: One chemist suggested the droplets carry that irritant to your eyes.
beats.visual: Back above the counter: the droplet fan rises toward a stylised eye line at frame edge; a dotted arrow links them, drawn dashed to read as a theory. Slow overhead tilt-free hold.

beats.vo: The tough outer skin lets the flesh under it get squeezed first. Then it bursts.
beats.visual: Cross-section of an onion layer: tough skin as a firm Cast-Iron-dark band, the soft flesh below visibly compressing, then rupturing in a spray. Side-on macro, steady.

beats.vo: A blunter knife makes it worse. So do faster cuts.
beats.visual: Split frame: left a rounded blunt blade, right a razor edge, both hitting onion halves at once; the blunt side throws a wider spray. Locked-off split.

beats.vo: A sharper blade gave fewer, slower droplets.
beats.visual: The sharp side of the split holds alone, its thin spray settling. Slow push-in on the clean cut.

beats.vo: But the team tracked droplets, not tears.
beats.visual: Overhead on the counter: a small card slides in with 'droplets ✓' and 'tears ?' in Cast Iron on Butter. Static overhead.

beats.vo: And it's one study, still a preprint.
beats.visual: Same card; a second line stamps in beneath it. Hold still, no move.

beats.vo: The Pan Theory: sharpen your knife tonight. Fewer droplets, and maybe fewer tears.
beats.visual: Signature card on Countertop beige: 'The Pan Theory:' in Rubik, key word 'sharpen' in Tomato red on a Butter highlight. Overhead onion and a clean-cut half behind; hold 1 s.

end_card.text: The Pan Theory: sharpen your knife tonight. Fewer droplets, and maybe fewer tears.
